name: The Mughal Empire
title: Social Hierarchy of the Mughal Empire: From Emperor to Enslaved

tiers.name: The emperor
tiers.you: You grant and take away every noble’s rank and income and hear appeals as the final judge, but your sons command armies of their own and may fight each other, or you, for your throne.
tiers.kid: The Mughal emperor gave every noble his rank, and when he died his sons often fought each other for the throne.
tiers.rise: Only a prince of the dynasty, descended from Timur, could reign, and the throne went to the son who won the struggle that followed an emperor’s illness or death. Akbar came to it in 1556, aged thirteen, under the regent Bairam Khan.
tiers.why: The emperor, the pādshāh, was the source of every rank.

tiers.name: Ranked nobles and officers
tiers.you: You hold a numbered rank, keep a troop of horsemen ready for the emperor, and collect the revenue of villages assigned to you until he moves you on, every three or four years.
tiers.kid: Mughal nobles held numbered ranks that showed how many horsemen they had to keep ready for the emperor.
tiers.rise: A newcomer needed a patron to present him to the paymaster general and money for horses and men; promotions came at festivals, on campaigns or for a handsome present. No rank or title was inherited, but sons of the service, the khanazads, held nearly half the high ranks under Aurangzeb.
tiers.why: Under the mansabdari system every officer of the empire above the lowest levels, judges apart, held a mansab, a numbered rank in one service that was army, nobility and civil government at once.

tiers.name: Landholders and chiefs
tiers.you: You hold the hereditary right to collect the revenue of your villages and keep a share of it, and you lead armed kinsmen who may one day hold your fort against the emperor’s troops.
tiers.kid: Zamindars were local landholders and chiefs who collected taxes from farmers and kept part for themselves.
tiers.rise: Zamindari rights passed by inheritance, though the choice of heir depended in part on the emperor’s pleasure. A chief who submitted might be given a mansab; in eastern Bengal Isa Khan accepted only a nominal Mughal overlordship and kept his autonomy.
tiers.why: The zamindars held hereditary rights over the revenue of the land, and the word covered men of very different weight.

tiers.name: Religious scholars and holy men
tiers.you: You teach the law or keep a holy man’s shrine and live on a tax-free grant of revenue from the emperor, which a new reign or a new policy can take away.
tiers.kid: Muslim scholars and judges, Sufi holy men and Hindu priests called Brahmins were honoured for their learning.
tiers.rise: Muslim scholars rose by learning and patronage, and a trained jurist could be appointed qazi by the emperor or the sadr. Brahmin rank came by birth, and some Brahmins lived as landholders, officials or farmers instead.
tiers.why: Learning and holiness formed a rank of their own in both great faiths.

tiers.name: Merchants and bankers
tiers.you: You deal in spices, bullion and coral through agents in many cities and lend to the European companies, but a governor can jail you and raiders can strip your warehouses.
tiers.kid: Mughal merchants and bankers grew rich from trade and sent money between distant cities using written bills.
tiers.rise: Trade and banking ran in families and communities. A few merchants crossed into the imperial service, as the Persian diamond trader Mir Jumla II did, rising to be a Mughal general and governor of Bengal; extortion by officials or a raid could ruin a house.
tiers.why: The great merchants and bankers were rich, and the empire’s silver economy ran through their hands.

tiers.name: Artisans and townspeople
tiers.you: You weave cloth or work metal at a trade your family has followed for generations, sell to merchants who ship your goods across the seas, and earn low wages.
tiers.kid: Mughal weavers made fine cotton cloth, such as muslin, that people bought all over Asia and Europe.
tiers.rise: Most artisans followed the craft of their family and jati. The most skilled could find work in the imperial workshops, and people moved to wherever the court and its demand went.
tiers.why: Mughal India had many large towns: under Akbar, Nizamuddin Ahmad counted 120 great cities and 3,200 townships, and Agra, Lahore and Delhi may each have held several hundred thousand people.

tiers.name: Peasants
tiers.you: You till fields your family has a hereditary right to farm, owe the state a third or more of your crop in cash, and grow cotton or indigo for sale as well as grain to eat.
tiers.kid: Most people in Mughal India were farmers who grew wheat, rice and cotton and paid heavy taxes on their harvests.
tiers.rise: Clearing new land earned a peasant tax-free years; a heavy demand could drive a family from its fields, and revenue officers could even enslave peasants who failed to pay.
tiers.why: The peasants, the raiyat, were the great majority and paid for the empire.

tiers.name: The lowest castes
tiers.you: You were born into a caste that the higher castes treat as untouchable; you tan hides, sweep or work other men’s fields, for your family holds no land of its own.
tiers.kid: People of the lowest castes were kept apart by higher castes and did work such as tanning leather and sweeping.
tiers.rise: Caste came by birth. Devotional movements that rejected caste, like those of Ravidas and the Satnamis, offered dignity and community, though not a higher rank.
tiers.why: Below the peasants stood the castes that Brahmin texts placed outside the four varnas altogether and that higher castes treated as untouchable, because their hereditary work, such as tanning hides and sweeping, was…

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You were taken in war or seized for unpaid revenue and now serve in a great household; you may not inherit, testify in court or marry without your owner’s leave, though your owner may free you.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people were owned by others and made to work without pay, mostly as servants in rich households.
tiers.rise: Freedom came by manumission, in whole or in part, under rules the jurists set out. Slave soldiers could rise far: in the neighbouring Ahmadnagar Sultanate the Ethiopian Malik Ambar, brought to India as a slave, became regent and led the Deccan’s resistance to the Mughals.
tiers.why: Slavery in Mughal India was mostly domestic.
